claim: The cerebellum has been implicated in the regulation of social behavior.
source: The cerebellum has been implicated in the regulation of social behavior.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by citations in the introduction section.

claim: The cerebellum's influence on social behavior is thought to arise from communication, via the thalamus, to forebrain regions integral in the expression of social interactions, including the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC).
source: Its influence is thought to arise from communication, via the thalamus, to forebrain regions integral in the expression of social interactions, including the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC).
evidence: This claim is based on established anatomical connectivity and is supported by citations in the manuscript.

claim: The E-Scope is an electrophysiology-integrated miniature microscope that can synchronously measure extracellular electrical activity in the cerebellum along with calcium imaging of the ACC.
source: We developed the E-Scope, an electrophysiology-integrated miniature microscope, to synchronously measure extracellular electrical activity in the cerebellum along with calcium imaging of the ACC.
evidence: The manuscript describes the development and capabilities of the E-Scope device.

claim: During social interactions, a significant subpopulation of cerebellar Purkinje cells (PCs) in right Crus I were robustly inhibited.
source: We found that during social interactions a significant subpopulation of cerebellar PCs were robustly inhibited
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by electrophysiological recordings presented in the results.

claim: Most modulated neurons in the dentate nucleus (DN) were activated during social interactions.
source: while most modulated neurons in the DN were activated
evidence: This finding is supported by electrophysiological data from DN recordings during social behavior.

claim: The activity of activated DN neurons was correlated with positively modulated ACC neurons during social interactions.
source: and their activity was correlated with positively modulated ACC neurons.
evidence: Correlation analysis between DN and ACC neurons is presented in the results section.

claim: The distinctions in correlated activity between cerebellar and ACC neurons largely disappeared when only non-social epochs were analyzed.
source: These distinctions largely disappeared when only non-social epochs were analyzed suggesting that cerebellar-cortical interactions were behaviorally specific.
evidence: This is supported by comparative analysis of social vs. non-social epochs in the results.

claim: Cerebellar stroke or injury could result in personality changes, blunted affect, and even antisocial behavior.
source: Early studies showed that cerebellar stroke or injury could result in personality changes, blunted affect, and even antisocial behavior (Schmahmann and Sherman, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Schmahmann and Sherman, 1998.

claim: The cerebellum contributes to elements of social cognition including 'mentalizing' or 'mirroring'.
source: More recent studies using neuroimaging and behavioral assays indicate the cerebellum contributes to elements of social cognition including 'mentalizing' or 'mirroring' (Van Overwalle et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Van Overwalle et al., 2020.

claim: Modulating the neural activity of cerebellar PCs through the insertion of disease related gene mutations or chemogenetic alterations of firing rate reduced social interactions.
source: Modulating the neural activity of cerebellar PCs through the insertion of disease related gene mutations or chemogenetic alterations of firing rate reduced social interactions (Badura et al., 2018; Kelly et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Badura et al., 2018 and Kelly et al., 2020.

claim: Optogenetic suppression of cerebellar output to the forebrain or midbrain, especially cerebellar neurons projecting to the ventral tegmental area (VTA), decreased social interest.
source: Moreover, optogenetic suppression of cerebellar output to the forebrain or midbrain, especially cerebellar neurons projecting to the ventral tegmental area (VTA), decreased social interest (Carta et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Carta et al., 2019.

claim: Among all cerebellar regions, modulation of the RCrus I of the cerebellar cortex had the most significant impact on the expression of social behavior.
source: Among all cerebellar regions, modulation of the RCrus I of the cerebellar cortex had the most significant impact on the expression of social behavior (Stoodley et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Stoodley et al., 2017.

claim: The RCrus I PC axons project to the DN, which in turn innervates the ventromedial thalamic neurons.
source: These socially relevant brain regions have known multisynaptic connectivity, in which the RCrus I PC axons project to the DN, which in turn innervates the ventromedial thalamic neurons (Badura et al., 2018; Kelly et al., 2020).
evidence: This anatomical connectivity is supported by citations to Badura et al., 2018 and Kelly et al., 2020.

claim: Targeted lesions to the ACC in non-human primates and selective gene deletion in mice decreased sociability and the recognition of social and emotional cues.
source: The cerebellum's interactions with the ACC are of interest as targeted lesions to it in non-human primates and most recently, selective gene deletion in mice, decreased sociability and the recognition of social and emotional cues (Devinsky et al., 1995; Guo et al., 2019; Hadland et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Devinsky et al., 1995; Guo et al., 2019; and Hadland et al., 2003.

claim: The E-Scope uses a single coaxial cable that minimally impacts animal movement to integrate both imaging and electrophysiological data streams along with the Miniscope's power.
source: This 'E-Scope' uses a single coaxial cable that minimally impacts animal movement to integrate both imaging and electrophysiological data streams along with the Miniscope's power.
evidence: This describes a technical feature of the E-Scope device.

claim: The electrophysiological component of the E-Scope is especially advantageous for brain regions with high basal firing rate neurons, such as the cerebellum, where activity may be obscured or not amenable to calcium imaging.
source: The electrophysiological component of this dual neural activity monitoring system is especially advantageous for brain regions with high basal firing rate neurons, such as the cerebellum, where activity may be obscured or not amenable to calcium imaging.
evidence: This is a reasoning about the advantages of the E-Scope based on known properties of cerebellar neurons.

claim: The E-Scope weighs less than 4.5 g.
source: The entire assembly weighs less than 4.5 g.
evidence: This is a measured specification of the device.

claim: For each mouse, approximately 200 ACC neurons were recorded using calcium imaging.
source: For each mouse, we recorded approximately 200 ACC neurons using calcium imaging (Figure 1D)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the recordings, with reference to Figure 1D.

claim: For each mouse, 1–9 cerebellar neurons were recorded using dense electrode arrays.
source: and 1–9 cerebellar neurons using dense electrode arrays (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the recordings, with reference to Figure 1E.

claim: Purkinje cells were identified by the presence of complex spikes (CS) along with the simple spikes (SS) in the recordings.
source: P-sort open-source software was used for PCs, which were identified by the presence of complex spikes (CS) along with the simple spikes (SS) in the recordings (Figure 1G; Sedaghat-Nejad et al., 2021).
evidence: This describes the method for identifying PCs, supported by reference to Figure 1G and a citation.

claim: Recorded animals made more contact with the other mouse than with the object.
source: Recorded animals made more contact with the other mouse than with the object (Figure 2A)
evidence: This is a behavioral observation supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Nearly one-third of the PCs (28.5%, n=8) were robustly inhibited by social interaction.
source: Nearly one-third of the PCs (28.5%, n=8) were robustly inhibited by social interaction (Figure 2D, E and G)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the electrophysiological recordings, with reference to Figure 2D, E, and G.

claim: Only three PCs (10.7%) were excited during social interaction.
source: while only three PCs (10.7%) were excited during social interaction (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the recordings, with reference to Figure 2D.

claim: Neurons inhibited by social interaction were inhibited for 1–3 s.
source: Neurons inhibited by social interaction were inhibited for 1–3 s (Figure 2C and E)
evidence: This is a temporal characteristic of the inhibition observed in the data, with reference to Figure 2C and E.

claim: The inhibition of PCs during social interaction was far longer than the SS pause typically induced by CSs (up to ~40 ms).
source: which was far longer than the SS pause is typically induced by CSs (up to ~40 ms) (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is a comparison between observed inhibition duration and known CS-induced pauses, with reference to Figure 1G.

claim: Out of 99 DN neurons recorded, 20 neurons (20.2%) were excited during social interaction.
source: Out of 99 DN neurons recorded, 20 neurons (20.2%) were excited during social interaction (Soc + DN)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from DN recordings.

claim: 12 DN neurons (12.1%) were inhibited during social interaction.
source: 12 neurons (12.1%) were inhibited (Soc– DN)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from DN recordings.

claim: 67 DN neurons were not significantly modulated by social interaction.
source: and the remaining 67 not significantly modulated (nsDN) (Figure 2I–N).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from DN recordings, with reference to Figure 2I-N.

claim: The excitation of DN neurons during social interaction was more robust than inhibition and firing rates were increased for 2–4 s post interaction onset.
source: The excitation was more robust than inhibition and firing rates were increased for 2–4 s post interaction onset.
evidence: This describes characteristics of DN neuron responses during social interaction.

claim: DN cells recorded in the object interaction sessions (n=85) showed smaller responses compared to the social interaction with 10 (11.7%) and 6 (7.05%) excited and inhibited units, respectively.
source: The DN cells recorded in the object interaction sessions (n=85) showed smaller responses compared to the social interaction with 10 (11.7%) and 6 (7.05%) excited and inhibited units, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a comparative finding between social and object interactions, with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: DN neurons did not show any difference in mean firing rate between Soc+ and Soc– groups.
source: DN neurons did not show any difference (F=1.589, p=0.2172) in mean firing rate between Soc+ and Soc– groups
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the analysis of DN neuron firing rates.

claim: PCs showed a clear difference in mean firing rate between the Soc+ and Soc– groups.
source: However, PCs showed a clear difference (F=5.742, p=0.04) in mean firing rate between the two socially responding types (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C,D).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the analysis of PC firing rates, with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 3C,D.

claim: Mice tended to reduce their speed and head angular velocity upon social interaction.
source: In the sessions recorded, we found mice tended to reduce their speed and head angular velocity upon interaction (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A, B).
evidence: This is a behavioral observation from the recordings, with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 4A, B.

claim: Soc+ and Soc– PCs as well as DN neurons showed no significant change in activity upon onset or offset of locomotion.
source: Analysis of the Soc+ and Soc– PCs as well as DN neurons showed no significant change in activity upon onset (Figure 2—figure supplement 4C, D) or offset (Figure 2—figure supplement 4E, F) of locomotion.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of movement-related activity, with references to Figure 2—figure supplement 4C-F.

claim: Head rotation onset had no relationship to PC or DN activity in Soc+ or Soc– groups.
source: In addition, head rotation onset had no relationship to PC or DN activity in Soc+ or Soc– groups (Figure 2—figure supplement 4G, H).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of head rotation-related activity, with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 4G, H.

claim: The activity changes observed in cerebellar neurons at the onset of social interactions are unlikely to be related to motor aspects of behavior during social interactions.
source: Therefore, the activity changes we observed in cerebellar neurons at the onset of social interactions are unlikely to be related to motor aspects of behavior during social interactions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of correlation between cerebellar activity and movement parameters.

claim: The electrophysiological responses in the cerebellum during social interaction are predominantly composed of PC inhibition and DN excitation.
source: Overall, the electrophysiological responses in the cerebellum during social interaction are predominantly composed of PC inhibition and DN excitation.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from cerebellar recordings.

claim: The results are consistent with the cerebellar anatomical circuit, where simultaneously decreased PC activity would be predicted to disinhibit DNs, thus resulting in excitatory output from the cerebellum to downstream brain areas.
source: These results are consistent with the cerebellar anatomical circuit, where simultaneously decreased PC activity would be predicted to disinhibit DNs, thus resulting in excitatory output from the cerebellum to downstream brain areas (Lee et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results in the context of known cerebellar circuitry, supported by a citation to Lee et al., 2015.

claim: 4868 ACC neurons were recorded during social interaction sessions.
source: We recorded 4868 and 3149 neurons during social and object interaction sessions, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from ACC calcium imaging recordings.

claim: 3149 ACC neurons were recorded during object interaction sessions.
source: We recorded 4868 and 3149 neurons during social and object interaction sessions, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from ACC calcium imaging recordings.

claim: 3.6% of ACC neurons were socially excited (Soc + ACC).
source: Of the recorded cells, 3.6% of ACC neurons were socially excited (Soc + ACC; Figure 3B, D and F)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from ACC recordings, with reference to Figure 3B, D, and F.

claim: 5.2% of ACC neurons were socially inhibited (Soc– ACC).
source: and 5.2% were socially inhibited (Soc– ACC; Figure 3C, E and F).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from ACC recordings, with reference to Figure 3C, E, and F.

claim: The proportions of socially modulated ACC neurons were greater than what would be expected by chance given the criteria for AUC significance (p<0.025).
source: These proportions were greater than what would be expected by chance given the criteria for AUC significance (p<0.025).
evidence: This is a statistical interpretation of the significance of the observed proportions.

claim: 4.1% of ACC neurons were excited by object interactions.
source: Conversely, 4.1% and 8.4% of ACC neurons were excited or inhibited by object interactions, respectively (Figure 3G and H, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from ACC recordings during object interactions, with reference to Figure 3G, H, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: 8.4% of ACC neurons were inhibited by object interactions.
source: Conversely, 4.1% and 8.4% of ACC neurons were excited or inhibited by object interactions, respectively (Figure 3G and H, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from ACC recordings during object interactions, with reference to Figure 3G, H, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The overlap of neurons significantly excited by both social and object interactions was 0.1% of all neurons.
source: The overlap of neurons significantly excited or inhibited by both social and object interactions was 0.1% and 0.4% of all neurons, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding about the overlap between social and object-responsive neurons.

claim: The overlap of neurons significantly inhibited by both social and object interactions was 0.4% of all neurons.
source: The overlap of neurons significantly excited or inhibited by both social and object interactions was 0.1% and 0.4% of all neurons, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding about the overlap between social and object-responsive neurons.

claim: A significant proportion of non-overlapping ACC neurons were excited or inhibited by social and object interactions.
source: Therefore, a significant proportion of non-overlapping ACC neurons were excited or inhibited by social and object interactions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the low overlap percentages observed.

claim: ACC neuron activity showed no significant correlation with movement at the onset or offset of locomotion or head rotation.
source: Similar to our observation in the cerebellum, ACC activity showed no significant correlation with movement at the onset or offset of locomotion or head rotation (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of ACC activity in relation to movement, with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The cerebellum indirectly connects to the ACC via the ventral medial thalamus.
source: Previous reports indicate the cerebellum indirectly connects to the ACC via the ventral medial thalamus (Figure 4A), but it is not clear whether this indirect connection drives ACC firing during social bouts (Badura et al., 2018; Kelly et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an anatomical fact supported by citations to Badura et al., 2018 and Kelly et al., 2020, with reference to Figure 4A.

claim: Cerebellar PC and DN neurons and ACC neurons that were similarly modulated by social interaction showed higher correlation values compared to cell pairs that were modulated in opposite directions.
source: Overall, as expected, cerebellar PC and DN neurons and ACC neurons that were similarly modulated by social interaction showed higher correlation values compared to cell pairs that were modulated in opposite directions (Figure 4D–G).
evidence: This is a finding from correlation analysis, with reference to Figure 4D-G.

claim: The differences in correlation between similarly and oppositely modulated cell pairs almost entirely disappeared when only non-social epochs were analyzed.
source: Interestingly, these differences almost entirely disappeared when only non-social epochs were analyzed (Figure 4D–G insets).
evidence: This is a finding from comparative analysis of social vs. non-social epochs, with reference to Figure 4D-G insets.

claim: Correlated activity is largely driven by social interactions and not by the intrinsic connectivity of these neuronal groups.
source: These findings suggest that correlated activity is largely driven by social interactions and not by the intrinsic connectivity of these neuronal groups.
evidence: This is an inference based on the disappearance of correlation differences during non-social epochs.

claim: The majority of RCrus I PCs modulated by social interaction decrease their SS firing activity.
source: We show that the majority of RCrus I PCs modulated by social interaction decrease their SS firing activity.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from PC recordings.

claim: Most modulated DN neurons increased their firing rate during social interaction, consistent with disinhibition of DN firing by simultaneous decreases in PC SS firing rate.
source: Conversely, most modulated DN neurons increased their firing rate during social interaction, consistent with disinhibition of DN firing by simultaneous decreases in PC SS firing rate.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from DN recordings and an interpretation based on known circuitry.

claim: Less than 10% of ACC neurons were modulated by social interaction with the majority of neurons being inhibited.
source: In vivo calcium imaging during social interaction showed that less than 10 % of ACC neurons were modulated by social interaction with the majority of neurons being inhibited.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from ACC calcium imaging.

claim: Cerebellar and ACC neurons similarly modulated by social interaction showed higher correlations in their firing rate than cerebellar and ACC neurons that were modulated in opposite directions.
source: As expected, cerebellar and ACC neurons similarly modulated by social interaction showed higher correlations in their firing rate than cerebellar and ACC neurons that were modulated in opposite directions.
evidence: This is a summary of the correlation analysis findings.

claim: The differences in correlated firing largely disappeared when only non-social bouts were analyzed, indicating that correlations were dependent on social behavior and not on the intrinsic indirect connectivity of the two brain regions.
source: These differences in correlated firing largely disappeared when only non-social bouts were analyzed, indicating that correlations were dependent on social behavior and not on the intrinsic indirect connectivity of the two brain regions.
evidence: This is a summary of the main conclusion from the correlation analysis.

claim: Communication between the cerebellum and ACC is coordinating social behavior.
source: These results suggest that communication between the cerebellum and ACC is coordinating social behavior.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed correlations during social behavior.

claim: Open-source miniaturized microscopes have expanded access to calcium imaging tools and encouraged new developments in Miniscope technology.
source: Open-source miniaturized microscopes (Aharoni et al., 2019a; Cai et al., 2016) have expanded access to this tool and encouraged new developments in Miniscope technology including the development of wire-free (Shuman et al., 2020) and large field of view miniaturized microscopes (Guo et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a statement about the impact of open-source microscopes, supported by multiple citations.

claim: The NINscope was developed for multi-region recording of calcium signals, allowing simultaneous calcium imaging complex spike activity in the cerebellum and motor cortical activity during free behavior.
source: In recent years, a miniaturized microscope called the NINscope was developed for multi-region recording of calcium signals (de Groot et al., 2020), allowing simultaneous calcium imaging complex spike activity in the cerebellum and motor cortical activity during free behavior.
evidence: This describes the capabilities of the NINscope, supported by a citation to de Groot et al., 2020.

claim: Calcium imaging in PCs provides only a partial picture of their activity, as it reports only the rate of CSs, but not the dynamic and persistent SS firing that is characteristic of these fast-spiking neurons.
source: However, calcium imaging in PCs provides only a partial picture of their activity, as it reports only the rate of CSs, but not the dynamic and persistent SS firing that is characteristic of these fast-spiking neurons.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of calcium imaging in PCs based on known properties of PC firing.

claim: The E-Scope can synchronously acquire calcium imaging data from one area and electrophysiological data from another to allow simultaneous examination and integration of electrical, calcium, and behavioral data streams.
source: Here, we introduce the E-Scope, which can synchronously acquire calcium imaging data from one area and electrophysiological data from another to allow simultaneous examination and integration of electrical, calcium, and behavioral data streams.
evidence: This describes the capabilities of the E-Scope device.

claim: The E-Scope provides method flexibility, allowing simultaneous recordings with areas where implanting a lens may be too invasive, such as deep brain regions like the DN where lens implantation would require the removal of its input layer in the cerebellar cortex.
source: The E-Scope also provides method flexibility, allowing simultaneous recordings with areas where implanting a lens may be too invasive, such as deep brain regions like the DN where lens implantation would require the removal of its input layer in the cerebellar cortex.
evidence: This describes an advantage of the E-Scope based on anatomical considerations.

claim: The E-Scope can be used to record local field potentials from any brain region, regardless of depth, simultaneously with calcium imaging.
source: Furthermore, the E-Scope can be used to record local field potentials from any brain region, regardless of depth, simultaneously with calcium imaging.
evidence: This describes a capability of the E-Scope.

claim: The integration of data streams and Miniscope power into a thin single coax cable is less limiting to the physical movement of the animal than multiple wires, enabling better interpretation of physiological correlates of behavior.
source: Additionally, the integration of data streams and Miniscope power into a thin single coax cable is less limiting to the physical movement of the animal than multiple wires, enabling better interpretation of physiological correlates of behavior.
evidence: This describes an advantage of the E-Scope design.

claim: The E-Scope can be used with multiple different extracellular electrophysiological recording techniques including silicon microprobes, tetrode arrays, or flexible electrode arrays.
source: Moreover, the E-Scope can be used with multiple different extracellular electrophysiological recording techniques including silicon microprobes as shown here, as well as tetrode arrays (Howe and Blair, 2022) or flexible electrode arrays (Chung et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes the versatility of the E-Scope, supported by citations.

claim: Cerebellar abnormalities are one of the most replicated anatomical changes in brains of individuals with autism.
source: In fact, cerebellar abnormalities are one of the most replicated anatomical changes in brains of individuals with autism (Fatemi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a statement about autism neuropathology, supported by a citation to Fatemi et al., 2012.

claim: This study is the first to demonstrate physiological cerebellar PC and DN neuron activity during social interaction in freely behaving animals.
source: Our study is the first to demonstrate physiological cerebellar PC and DN neuron activity during social interaction in freely behaving animals.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study.

claim: Most socially modulated PC neurons in RCrus I are inhibited.
source: We find that most socially modulated PC neurons in RCrus I are inhibited.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from PC recordings.

claim: One potential mechanism for PC inhibition could be coordinated decreases in cerebellar granule cell activity during social interaction dynamically decreasing excitatory input to PCs and, therefore, reducing PC SS firing.
source: One potential mechanism could be coordinated decreases in cerebellar granule cell activity during social interaction dynamically decreasing excitatory input to PCs and, therefore, reducing PC SS firing.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism proposed to explain the observed PC inhibition.

claim: Inhibition of PC firing rate may be due to an increase in inhibitory versus excitatory input from molecular layer interneurons (MLIs) versus granule cells, respectively.
source: Alternatively, inhibition of PC firing rate may be due to an increase in inhibitory versus excitatory input from molecular layer interneurons (MLIs) versus granule cells, respectively.
evidence: This is an alternative speculative mechanism proposed to explain the observed PC inhibition.

claim: Sensory stimulation can increase MLI activity.
source: Previous in vivo studies have shown that sensory stimulation can increase MLI activity (Jörntell and Ekerot, 2003)
evidence: This is a statement about MLI activity supported by a citation to Jörntell and Ekerot, 2003.

claim: Social sensory input such as olfactory stimuli could potentially increase MLI firing.
source: and, therefore, social sensory input such as olfactory stimuli could potentially increase MLI firing.
evidence: This is a speculative extension of the previous claim about MLI activity.

claim: Suppression of Crus I MLIs causes changes in social preference.
source: This potential mechanism of PC inhibition is supported by experiments where suppression of Crus I MLIs causes changes in social preference (Badura et al., 2018)
evidence: This is a statement about the role of MLIs in social behavior, supported by a citation to Badura et al., 2018.

claim: Bidirectional modulation of activity in the cerebellum is a well-known phenomenon.
source: Bidirectional modulation of activity in the cerebellum is a well-known phenomenon (De Zeeuw, 2021).
evidence: This is a statement about cerebellar physiology, supported by a citation to De Zeeuw, 2021.

claim: Bidirectional modulation of PC firing during social interaction was found with the majority of PCs inhibited by social interaction and a minority excited.
source: We found bidirectional modulation of PC firing during social interaction with the majority of PCs inhibited by social interaction and a minority excited.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings on PC modulation.

claim: Consistent with the inhibitory role of PCs onto DNs, the ratio of excited to inhibited neurons is inverted in DNs with the majority of modulated DNs excited and only minority inhibited.
source: Consistent with the inhibitory role of PCs onto DNs, we find this ratio to be inverted in DNs with the majority of modulated DNs excited and only minority inhibited.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the DN findings in the context of known PC-DN connectivity.

claim: Movement of the animal at the onset, offset, or changes in locomotion direction could not explain the modulations of activity recorded in the cerebellum.
source: Movement of the animal at the onset, offset, or changes in locomotion direction could not explain the modulations of activity we recorded in the cerebellum, suggesting that activity modulations were driven specifically by social interaction.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the analysis of movement-related activity.

claim: There was little overlap in the neurons modulated by social interaction and by object interactions.
source: In addition, there was little overlap in the neurons modulated by social interaction and by object interactions.
evidence: This is a finding from the comparison of social and object interaction responses.

claim: RCrus I activity is responsive to elements of social interaction itself.
source: This indicates that RCrus I activity is responsive to elements of social interaction itself, although the specific information encoded is still to be ascertained.
evidence: This is an inference based on the specificity of responses to social vs. object interactions.

claim: An indirect connection links RCrus I cerebellum to ACC via the thalamus.
source: An indirect connection links RCrus I cerebellum to ACC via the thalamus (Badura et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an anatomical fact supported by a citation to Badura et al., 2018.

claim: DN neurons project to the ventromedial thalamus, which in turn projects to the ACC.
source: DN neurons project to the ventromedial thalamus, which in turn projects to the ACC (de Lima et al., 2022; Kuramoto et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an anatomical fact supported by citations to de Lima et al., 2022 and Kuramoto et al., 2015.

claim: Correlations between PCs or DNs with ACC neurons are greater when these neurons are similarly modulated by social interaction.
source: As expected, we find that correlations between PCs or DNs with ACC neurons are greater when these neurons are similarly modulated by social interaction.
evidence: This is a finding from the correlation analysis.

claim: Differences in correlations disappear when only non-social epochs are analyzed, suggesting that spontaneous activity during non-social behavior and the intrinsic connectivity of the two regions is not sufficient to impose differences in correlations without social interaction.
source: However, these differences in correlations disappear when only non-social epochs are analyzed, suggesting that spontaneous activity during non-social behavior and the intrinsic connectivity of the two regions is not sufficient to impose differences in correlations without social interaction.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of correlations during social vs. non-social epochs.

claim: The cerebellum plays a role in social behavior.
source: Our findings support the theory that the cerebellum plays a role in social behavior.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the overall findings of the study.

claim: The E-Scope provides an important tool for examining the activity of two distant brain regions during behavior.
source: Moreover, the E-Scope provides an important tool for examining the activity of two distant brain regions during behavior.
evidence: This is a statement about the utility of the E-Scope.

claim: The study has uncovered how cerebellar activity indirectly impacts ACC neurons output during social behavior and non-social behavior.
source: We have further uncovered how cerebellar activity indirectly impacts ACC neurons output during social behavior and non-social behavior.
evidence: This is a summary of the main contribution of the study.

claim: These physiological insights into cerebellar and ACC communication during social behavior may eventually provide ways to finely tune cerebellar activity in autism models and eventually in humans to augment and improve the quality of social interactions.
source: These physiological insights into cerebellar and ACC communication during social behavior may eventually provide ways to finely tune cerebellar activity in autism models and eventually in humans to augment and improve the quality of social interactions.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential future applications of the findings.

claim: A two-shank, 64 channel silicon probe (64 H with 32 channels activated) was used for electrophysiological recordings.
source: A two-shank, 64 channel silicon probe (64 H with 32 channels activated) was used that was wire bonded and epoxied onto a probe PCB (PCB: Hughes Circuits, assembly: IDAX Microelectronics).
evidence: This describes the electrophysiological recording hardware used in the study.

claim: The Ephys PCB incorporated a 32-channel electrophysiology-integrated chip (Intan, RHD2132) and a 32-bit ARM-Cortex microcontroller unit (MCU).
source: This Ephys PCB incorporated a 32-channel electrophysiology-integrated chip (Intan, RHD2132) and a 32-bit ARM-Cortex microcontroller unit (MCU) (Atmel; ATSAMS70N21A).
evidence: This describes the components of the Ephys PCB.

claim: The MCU configures the Intan electrophysiology chip and polls it using direct memory access (DMA) over a single-ended serial peripheral interface (SPI) at up to 20 kSps per channel for new electrophysiology data across its 32 channels.
source: This MCU configures the Intan electrophysiology chip and polls it using direct memory access (DMA) over a single-ended serial peripheral interface (SPI) at up to 20 kSps per channel for new electrophysiology data across its 32 channels.
evidence: This describes the technical operation of the MCU in the E-Scope.

claim: 6–8 week-old C57BL/6 J young adult male mice at the time of initial surgery were used for in vivo E-Scope calcium imaging and electrophysiology experiments.
source: 6–8 week-old C57BL/6 J young adult male mice at the time of initial surgery were used for in vivo E-Scope calcium imaging and electrophysiology experiments.
evidence: This describes the animal subjects used in the study.

claim: All mice were acquired from Jackson Laboratories and group-housed three per cage on a 12 hr light-dark cycle.
source: All mice were acquired from Jackson Laboratories and group-housed three per cage on a 12 hr light-dark cycle.
evidence: This describes the housing conditions of the animals.

claim: All experimental protocols were approved by the Chancellor's Animal Research Committee of the University of California, Los Angeles in accordance with the U.S. National Institutes of Health (NIH) guidelines.
source: All experimental protocols were approved by the Chancellor's Animal Research Committee of the University of California, Los Angeles in accordance with the U.S. National Institutes of Health (NIH) guidelines.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval for the study.

claim: AAV1. Syn.GCaMP6f.WPRE.SV40 virus (titer 4.5 × 1013 GC/mL; Penn Vector Core) was injected for Miniscope calcium imaging experiments.
source: For Miniscope calcium imaging experiments, AAV1. Syn.GCaMP6f.WPRE.SV40 virus (titer 4.5 × 1013 GC/mL; Penn Vector Core) was injected.
evidence: This describes the viral vector used for calcium imaging.

claim: Proximity to each other's body was used as a measure of social interaction.
